title: Fix off-by-one in `chunk`

description.text: A teammate wrote `chunk(arr, size)` to split rows into smaller batches. It looks fine at first glance, but the loop boundary is slightly off: exact divisions can produce an extra empty chunk, and an empty input can come back as `[[]]`. Fix the bug without changing the function's contract.

title: Stop mutating caller data in `unique`

description.text: A teammate tried to make `unique(arr)` look clever with a one-liner. The returned values seem close, but two subtle bugs slipped in: it reorders the data and it mutates the caller's array in place. Fix it so the helper keeps the first-seen order and does not change any shared input state.

title: Fix missing return in `map` / `filter`

description.text: A teammate refactored a simple array pipeline to use block-bodied arrow functions because it looked more readable. The shape still looks right, but now the result comes back empty or full of `undefined`. Fix the missing returns without changing the overall intent of the pipeline.
examples: summarizeOpenTickets([{ title: ' Bug ', open: true }, { title: 'Chore', open: false }]) // ['BUG']
summarizeOpenTickets([{ title: ' Docs ', open: true }, { title: ' Test ', open: true }]) // ['DOCS','TEST']

title: Fix wrong defaults in `normalizeSettings`

sources.label: Taro: Capital One senior frontend engineer interview, 2024
sources.note: The case round asked to find a bug in a budgeting program written by an intern, in Java, C++, Node.js or Python, without coding the fix. This drill practises finding a defaults bug in a teammate's helper; it is not the reported code.

description.text: A teammate used `||` while hydrating UI settings, and the bug stayed invisible until real saved values showed up. Now `0`, an intentionally blank subtitle, and `false` keep getting overwritten by defaults. Fix the helper so only truly missing values fall back.
examples: normalizeSettings({ retryCount: 0, subtitle: '', emailOptIn: false }) // { retryCount: 0, subtitle: '', emailOptIn: false }
normalizeSettings({ retryCount: undefined, subtitle: null, emailOptIn: undefined }) // { retryCount: 3, subtitle: 'Untitled', emailOptIn: true }

title: Fix numeric sort in `sortScores`

description.text: A teammate wrote a tiny leaderboard helper with plain `sort()`. It looked fine in a quick demo with single-digit values, then broke the moment scores like `10` and `100` showed up. Fix the bug so numbers sort numerically in ascending order while keeping the original input unchanged.

title: Fix lost `this` binding in callback registration

description.text: A teammate passes an object method straight into a callback API, assuming it will still remember its owner later. Direct calls like `tracker.recordClick()` work, but the same method breaks once another function invokes it without the original receiver. Fix the bug so registered callbacks keep the right `this`.

title: Fix stale closure in delayed autosave callback

description.text: A teammate tried to make autosave "predictable" by capturing the current draft when wiring a delayed callback. That feels reasonable until the user keeps typing: the callback keeps saving the old draft it closed over instead of the latest one. Fix the bug so delayed saves read fresh state at execution time.

title: Fix async race in `fetchWithCache`

description.text: A teammate built a shared fetch helper to avoid duplicate network work, but real traffic exposed two nasty bugs. Concurrent callers with the same key still fan out into multiple requests, and a failed request can leave the helper stuck in a bad in-flight state. Fix it so callers share one active request per key, successful responses cache correctly, and failures can retry cleanly.

title: Bug Squash: Fix an Unfamiliar Invoicing Repo

description.text: You joined the team that owns a small invoicing library: five files under `src/` you have not seen before. Support forwarded four reports. A $19.99 notebook is billed as $19.98. A $5.00 coupon wipes out the whole invoice. After an invoice is built, the cart it came from lists its items in a different order. And after a timeout, the payment service logged two charges for one invoice. Use the file tabs above the editor to read the code, find the cause of each report, and fix it without renaming an exported function or changing its arguments; the tests show what correct looks like. Accounts of the Stripe frontend onsite describe a bug squash round of this shape: finding and fixing bugs in a project you have not seen before.

solutionBlock.overview: Each report traces to one file, and no fix renames an exported function or changes its arguments. Follow each symptom down its call path: the $19.98 bill runs through `toMinorUnits`, the vanished invoice through `discountFor`, the reordered cart through `linesByAmount`, and the double charge through `payInvoice`. The doc comments state the contracts the bugs break: amounts are minor units, and one idempotency key covers every attempt at a payment.

approaches.title: Follow each report to its cause
approaches.prose:
1. **The lost cent** (`src/currency.js`): `19.99 * 100` is `1998.9999999999998` in floating point, and `Math.floor` drops it to 1998. Round to the nearest minor unit with `Math.round`; the yen test guards against hard-coding 100.
2. **The vanishing invoice** (`src/invoice.js`): `amountOff` is already in minor units, as the comment above `buildInvoice` says, but `discountFor` converts it again, so a 500-cent coupon is worth 50,000 and the total clamps to 0. Use `amountOff` as it is.
3. **The reordered cart** (`src/line-items.js`): `items.sort()` sorts the caller's array in place, so building an invoice reorders the cart. Sort a copy with `[...items].sort(...)`.
4. **The double charge** (`src/payments.js`): `createId('pay')` runs inside the retry loop, so each attempt sends a new idempotency key and the API cannot tell a retry from a new charge. Create the key once, before the loop. The declined-card test guards the other half: a decline is an answer, not a network failure, so it is not retried.

In the interview, say which report you take first and why, reproduce it with the failing test before you change code, and keep each fix in the one file that causes it.

pitfalls: Rounding money only for display, after a lost cent is already in the total.
Dividing the coupon by 100 in `buildInvoice` instead of removing the second conversion.
Copying the cart in `buildInvoice` and leaving `linesByAmount` to reorder its next caller's array.
Retrying every error: retrying a declined card changes nothing and hides the decline.
techniques: Work from the symptom to the call path to the contract before you touch code.
Keep money in integer minor units and convert once, where it enters.
Sort a copy, or use `toSorted()`, on data you do not own.
Create one idempotency key per operation and send it on every retry.

title: Case: Find the Bug in an Intern's Budget Summary

seo.h1IntentLabel: Find the bug in an intern's budget summary

description.text:
Capital One's Power Day case, as a 2024 senior account describes it: find the bug in a budgeting program written by an intern without coding the fix. This page runs the case in that order. Start it to work an example by hand, mark the lines you would change and say why while the code stays read-only, then compare with a sample answer. After that the workspace runs, and its tests check your fix.

The function behind the household dashboard summarizes one month. It turns each expense into a monthly amount: a monthly one as it is, a weekly one 52 times a year, a yearly one once. It rounds each monthly amount to cents and adds them up by category. It reports what was spent, what is left of the income and the savings rate as a whole percentage of the income, which is 0 for a month without income. And it flags every category whose monthly total goes over its limit, a limit of 0 included.

solutionBlock.overview: Work the example first: $100 of groceries a week is 100 × 52 / 12 = $433.33 a month, and the function says $400. Line 8 counts four weeks in every month, so each weekly cost is about 8% too low and the dashboard shows more money left than there is. The fix is amount * 52 / 12 with each monthly amount rounded to cents, which line 10 never does: 100 × 52 / 12 is 433.333…, and the worked example, the test that would have caught both, needs exactly $433.33. Two more lines break stated rules: a limit of 0 is never checked (line 17), and a month without income divides by zero (line 23).

approaches.title: Fix: monthly amounts in cents, every limit checked, no division by zero
approaches.prose: Convert each expense to whole cents per month: weekly ones as cents × 52 / 12, yearly ones as cents / 12, each rounded once. Totals, spending and what is left then add up exactly, and converting back to dollars at the end shows the same cents the dashboard prints. Check a category whenever it has a limit, so a limit of 0 counts, and return a savings rate of 0 when there is no income instead of dividing by it.

pitfalls: Reading the code before working an example: amount * 4 looks like "four weeks a month" and reads as right.
Rewriting the whole function in the case instead of naming the one line, the input that breaks it and the smallest fix.
Fixing the weekly rate and leaving the result unrounded: 433.3333 is not the $433.33 the dashboard shows.
Treating a limit of 0 as no limit: limits[category] && … is false for 0.
techniques: Restate the rule, then work one example by hand before you read a line of code.
Trace the function with the example values and write each variable down as it changes.
Name the bug as a line, an input that triggers it and the wrong output it produces.
Propose the smallest fix and one test that would have caught it, then mention the rarer risks briefly.
